steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The Greek Underworld (Hades) was the realm of the dead, ruled by the god Hades and his queen Persephone

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: All souls went to the Underworld — it was not simply a place of reward or punishment

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Charon the ferryman transported souls across the River Styx — the dead were buried with a coin for payment

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The Underworld had distinct regions: Asphodel Meadows for ordinary souls, Elysium for heroes, and Tartarus for the wicked

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: Why were the dead buried with a coin in their mouth? | Q: What were the three main regions of the Underworld? | Q: How did Persephone's story explain the seasons?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: To pay Charon the ferryman for transport across the River Styx — souls without payment were said to wander the banks for a hundred years. | The Asphodel Meadows (for ordinary souls), Elysium (for heroes and the favoured), and Tartarus (for the wicked and those who offended the gods). | Persephone was abducted by Hades and ate pomegranate seeds, binding her to the Underworld for part of each year. Her mother Demeter's grief caused winter; her return brought spring.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: When discussing the Underworld, always specify which region you mean — don't treat it as one place The Persephone myth is central — it connects the Underworld to Greek explanations of the natural world Use the Orpheus myth to illustrate themes of love, loss and the power and limits of music Katabasis episodes in Homer and Virgil are key literary evidence for Underworld beliefs Remember that Underworld beliefs evolved over time — early traditions were bleaker than later ones
